19.0.s.en: 1. David’s consolation over Nahash, king of the children of Ammon

19.0.0.en: 1 Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. 2 And David said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me.” And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him.

19.0.1.en: Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. [1]

19.0.2.en: The children of Ammon reached the peak of their power in the days of the judges, and David was the first military commander of the children of Israel to crush them, so they had no strength to cause trouble for Israel for many long years.

19.0.3.en: Nahash fought Israel in the days of Saul (1 Sam 11). He most likely rendered services to David in the days of Saul which were not recorded. For this reason David sent a delegation to comfort his son Hanun on the death of his father, but sadly Hanun treated them in an improper way.

19.1.0.en: And David said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me.”

19.1.1.en: And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father.

19.1.2.en: So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him. [2]

19.1.3.en: The Holy Bible does not state what kindness Nahash showed to David, but the two entered into a close friendship during the period of David’s flight from Saul, and there was enmity between Saul and Nahash[1].

19.1.4.en: The Assyrian inscriptions state that a king of Philistia by the name of Hanun paid tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser, and that he entered into war with Sargon[2].

19.2.s.en: 2. The counsel of the princes of the children of Ammon

19.2.0.en: 3 But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, “Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land?” 4 Wherefore Hanun took David’s servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. 5 Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, “Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.”

19.2.1.en: But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun,

19.2.2.en: “Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee?

19.2.3.en: are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land?” [3]

19.2.4.en: When David rebuked Saul because he listened to his wicked counselors who were stirring him up against David unjustly, David said to him: “As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked” (1 Sam 24:13). This is what King Hanun fell into, for he set up for himself wicked counselors, and they offered them out of what they had, which is evil. It is fitting for leaders not to incline their ears to the counsels of the wicked. It was fitting for the king not to think ill; together with wisdom and caution, it is fitting for us not to be hasty in thinking ill of others.

19.3.0.en: Wherefore Hanun took David’s servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. [4]

19.3.1.en: Shaving the beard, especially a part of it, and tearing the garments in the middle, for someone against his will, was considered among the Jews and among Easterners in general a grave insult, a severe contempt and a challenge.

19.3.2.en: This view still exists in Egypt to this day, especially in the villages.

19.4.0.en: Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served.

19.4.1.en: And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed.

19.4.2.en: And the king said, “Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.” [5]

19.4.3.en: David the prophet presents to us a wonderful example of leaders who care for the dignity of those who work with them and carry out the service. He sent to meet them, because they were in shame, unable to meet anyone. He met them to raise their morale and to support them.

19.4.4.en: If David cared for those who worked with him so that no harm would befall them, how much more does the Lord of David care for His servants who suffer troubles and pains. If they accept crucifixion with Him with all joy, He grants them the power of the Resurrection, its joy and its glory.

19.5.s.en: 3. Hanun hires an army from Syria

19.5.0.en: 6 And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah. 7 So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. 8 And when David heard of it, he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. 9 And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come were by themselves in the field.

19.5.1.en: And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah. [6]

19.5.2.en: The story in this chapter concerning the alliance between the children of Ammon and the Syrians, and the victory over them, is found in (2 Sam 10).

19.5.3.en: Hanun king of Ammon and his counselors thought ill of David’s intentions, and so brought a disaster upon themselves, their country and the countries neighboring them.

19.5.4.en: Instead of Hanun’s acknowledging his rashness and folly in his conduct, he devoted a huge sum (a thousand talents of silver) to cover his error by entering into a failed battle.

19.5.5.en: Instead of David’s being the one who wanted war, it was the new king of the Ammonites who wanted this, and therefore he hired an army from Syria to help him against David, and we see here: 1. How the hearts of the wicked are hardened for their destruction, for the children of Ammon, when they saw that they had made themselves odious to David [1]. Instead of seeking peace and correcting what they had done, humbling themselves and seeking to satisfy David for the harm they had committed, behold, not only had they made themselves odious to David, but they also hated the justice of God, who is “King of nations,” who defends the right of the oppressed and keeps the violated laws of nations; indeed, they prepared for war and brought destruction upon themselves at the hands of David, which he had not intended for them. 2. How the courage of brave men increases in distress, for “when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind” [10], instead of thinking of retreat he redoubled his resolve, and although he could not double his army, he divided it, and he did not merely speak but acted, as a gallant man of great presence of mind; and when he saw himself surrounded, he agreed with his brother that each should help the other [12], and urged himself and his soldiers to act strongly, each in his position, with the aim of the glory of God and the good of their country, and not their own honor and personal benefit, and they left the matter to God: “and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight” [13]. 3. How the greatest arts of war that are aimed against justice and equity avail nothing, for the children of Ammon did all in their power to strengthen their position; they brought a mighty force into the field of battle and used it cunningly to the extent of their ability, yet because they were in the wrong and were defending falsehood, all this did not profit, and they were conquered in the most notorious defeat; for truth always prevails and triumphs in the end.

19.6.0.en: So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people;

19.6.1.en: who came and pitched before Medeba.

19.6.2.en: And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. [7]

19.6.3.en: The children of Ammon hired 32,000 chariots and also horsemen experienced in fighting with chariots, and also some infantry whom the text does not mention.

19.7.0.en: And when David heard of it, he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. [8]

19.7.1.en: David sent Joab and his brother Abishai with all the military forces against the forces of the children of Ammon allied with the Syrians, and they were victorious over them.

19.8.0.en: And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come were by themselves in the field. [9]

19.8.1.en: The army of the children of Ammon set out and drew up in array at the gate of the city, that is, outside the walls opposite Medeba on the border of the city of Arnon.

19.8.2.en: The Israelite army was alarmed by the Ammonites who were in front, and behind them the hired Syrian mercenaries. Joab determined to resist the mercenaries, and asked his brother Abishai to attack the Ammonites.

19.8.3.en: When the mercenaries were defeated, the courage of the Ammonites failed, and they were forced to flee[3].

19.9.s.en: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

19.9.0.en: 10 Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians. 11 And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set themselves in array against the children of Ammon. 12 And he said, “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. 13 Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight.” 14 So Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. 15 And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem. 16 And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers, and drew forth the Syrians that were beyond the river: and Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them. 17 And it was told David; and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set the battle in array against them. So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. 18 But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand chariots and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host.

19.9.1.en: The defeat of Aram reveals that the greatest arts of war that are aimed against justice and equity avail nothing.

19.9.2.en: Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians. [10]

19.9.3.en: If in the days of Saul none stood before Goliath the giant except the youth David the hero, now in the age of David there were many heroes standing before the giants of the hostile nations.

19.10.0.en: And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set themselves in array against the children of Ammon. [11]

19.11.0.en: And he said, “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. [12]

19.12.0.en: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight.” [13]

19.12.1.en: The secret of the success of Joab and his brother Abishai is that, while studying the situation with all seriousness and arranging the matter, they were confident in God to do what was for the good of the people: “let the LORD do that which is good in his sight” [13].

19.12.2.en: On the other hand, Joab supported his brother, urging him: “Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God.”

19.12.3.en: And it is remarkable that while they take pride in the people, ascribing them to themselves, “our people,” at the same time they ascribe the cities to God, “the cities of our God.” On the one hand they want to affirm their love for the people, and on the other hand God is the guardian of the people and their shepherd.

19.13.0.en: So Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. [14]

19.13.1.en: As Joab’s speech to his brother Abishai revealed their love for the people and their trust in the Lord, the enemy collapsed before them. Nothing shatters the power of the enemy of good like love for God and for the brethren. Therefore it is fitting for the believer, whether priest or of the people, to adorn himself or arm himself with love, so that the powers of darkness cannot prevail against him. By true love we fear neither the lusts of the flesh nor the lust of the love of the world, nor the devil and all his powers.

19.13.2.en: This love for God and for the brethren cannot be separated.

19.13.3.en: v He who fixes his mind on the love of God despises all things visible, even his own body becomes a stranger to him.

19.13.4.en: v He who sees a trace of hatred in his heart toward any man, through any fault whatever, makes himself altogether a stranger to the love of God, for the love of God cannot in any way cleave to hatred of man.

19.13.5.en: v Blessed is the man who learns to love all men equally.

19.13.6.en: v If you hate some people, and others you neither hate nor love, and some you love a little, and others you love much, you need to know from this variety in love that you are very far from perfect love, one of whose pillars is equality in love.

19.13.7.en: v He who loves God certainly loves his neighbor also. Such a person cannot hold fast to money, but rather, like God, gives it to everyone in need.

19.13.8.en: v When the mind begins to advance in the love of God, the demon of blasphemy begins to fight against it, suggesting to it strange, demonic thoughts; this happens because he bears a grudge against the new friend of God. And when the person thinks these thoughts about God, he feels shame and disgrace, and as a result he cannot draw near to God and pray. But by the power of God we gain the victory over him, and prevail over his wicked way, and are strengthened, and become more sincere in our love for Jesus. [His sword shall enter into his own heart, and his bows shall be broken] (Ps 37:15).

19.13.10.en: v O the greatness of love! Stronger than fire itself, it ascends to heaven itself, and there is none to hinder it[5].

19.13.11.en: v Paul, a citizen of heaven, a pillar of the Church, an earthly angel, a heavenly being. Like iron heated by fire becomes all aglow, so Paul was set aflame with love and became love itself[6].

19.14.0.en: And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city.

19.14.2.en: When Joab was victorious, his brother Abishai took courage and was victorious also. So if our sins cause our brethren to stumble, so that we are the cause of their fall, then our victory in the Lord supports our brethren so that they are strengthened and cleave to the Lord and are victorious with us!

19.14.3.en: With every victory you enjoy, you support your brother that he too may be victorious by God, his God.

19.15.0.en: And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers, and drew forth the Syrians that were beyond the river: and Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them. [16]

19.15.1.en: The Syrians sent to their kinsmen beyond the river and planned to take revenge on Israel. When David quickly realized the danger, he gathered his forces and took a defensive position. The arrogance of the Syrians fell, and they became servants to David.

19.16.0.en: And it was told David; and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set the battle in array against them.

19.16.1.en: So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. [17]

19.16.2.en: It seems in this chapter that David was sharp in temper, but he tried to live in peace. And we note here: 1. It is the disposition of godly people to be good neighbors, and especially to be thankful; David wanted to show kindness to Hanun as a neighbor, and because he remembered his father’s kindness to him; for those who receive kindness must repay it according to their ability when the opportunity arises, and those who receive from fathers must repay the sons after their departure. 2. It is “as saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked” (1 Sam 24:13); “for the vile person will speak villany... The instruments also of the churl are evil... to destroy... with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right” (Isa 32:6-7). So these lowly men who devise evil by themselves tend to jealousy and to thinking ill of others without cause. Hanun’s servants advised him that David’s messengers had come to spy out the land, as if a great man like David needed to do something mean like this; for if he had an evil intention against the Ammonites, he could have carried it out by force and not resorted to a base method; yet Hanun yielded to the opinion of his servants and, against the laws of nations, treated David’s messengers in a vile manner.

19.16.3.en: The children of Ammon were enemies of Israel, but David did not want to make war; he was on the defensive, as was the case with him for most of his life, for the man of God always finds himself on the defensive; we must put on the whole armor of God. What does this mean? Is it so that we may advance to war? No, but that we may stand ready, and this is what matters. 3. Leaders must protect their servants, and care for and attend to their affairs if harm befalls them in their service; David did so for his messengers [5], and the Lord Christ does likewise for His servants.

19.17.0.en: But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand chariots and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host. [18]

19.17.1.en: Those with whom God is not gather their strength again without the slightest profit; the Syrians had no interest in the matter at all, and served with the children of Ammon as mercenary soldiers, and when they were struck they thought of regaining their honor, and therefore sought help from the Syrians on the other bank of the Euphrates, but in vain, for they [fled before Israel] [18]. They lost seven thousand men, of whom it was said that they were men of seven hundred chariots (2 Sam 10:18).

19.18.s.en: 5. The submission of Hadarezer’s leaders to David

19.18.0.en: And when the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David, and served him.

19.18.1.en: Neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more. [19]

19.18.2.en: When the Syrians saw that Israel was the victor, they broke their alliance with the children of Ammon, “neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more” [19], and also made peace with David and became his servants. If only those who have stood in vain against God would return to themselves [and be reconciled to Him quickly while they are in the way] (Mt 5:25), and become His servants, for they have made themselves negligent if they become His enemies.

19.18.3.en: Grant me to flee from the counsel of the wicked

19.18.4.en: v From the wicked proceeds wickedness; protect me from them, that I may not incline my ear to them, but incline my ear to Your life-giving commandment.

19.18.5.en: v Because of the counsel of the wicked, Hanun the son of Nahash lost David’s friendship.

19.18.6.en: Instead of allying himself with David, so that the blessing of the Lord would come upon him, the evil of the wicked came upon him, and he paid for this a cost of this amount!

19.18.7.en: He lost his money, his chariots and his dignity.

19.18.8.en: v Hanun and his men insulted David’s messengers, so they hid in shame.

19.18.9.en: David, the man of the wide heart, cared with humility.

19.18.10.en: By his love, concern and care, he lifted their spirits.

19.18.11.en: And he did not allow any of his people to see them, so that no one would mock them.

19.18.12.en: v O Lord of David, all-loving, tender and kind.

19.18.13.en: Look upon Your servants and Your people.

19.18.14.en: You permit for a time the hand of the wicked to be stretched out against them.

19.18.15.en: But do not allow this hand to rest upon them.

19.18.16.en: Instead of mockery, pour out Your splendor upon them.

19.18.17.en: And instead of shame, reveal Your glory in them.

19.18.18.en: v Joab and his brother Abishai were strengthened to work on behalf of the Lord.

19.18.19.en: They trusted in God, so their lives were filled with strength, courage and hope.

19.18.20.en: And victory truly became their ally.

19.18.21.en: v Their wonderful love for their people was blended with God’s care for the people.

19.18.22.en: They took pride in the people, and called them “our people”!

19.18.23.en: They carried the people, as it were, on their hands before God, and so they realized God’s guarding of His people and the protection of their cities!
